Deep double descent

Test error can peak near interpolation before falling as capacity increases. Nakkiran et al., 2019 ↗

GeneralizationOptimizationScaling and capability prediction

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
V1As networks grow, test error can fall, peak near exact training fits, then fall. 878121

Suggested status Ccontested

The pattern appears in some experiments that vary network width and depends on training conditions and the evaluation metric, so its generality is contested. Networks trained without label noise can improve monotonically across interpolation, the point where a model fits the training data exactly.

Original resultNakkiran et al., 2019 ↗

The original study varied ResNet18 width on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using Adam.

After 4K training epochs on CIFAR-10 with 15% label noise, test error peaked near interpolation and declined as width increased further. With augmentation and no added label noise, CIFAR-100 showed a peak, while CIFAR-10 showed a plateau.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Architecture changes the benefits of capacity 55 studies

The benefit of added capacity depends on architecture, initialization, data structure and the solutions training selects. Parameter count alone does not order test risk.

  • At width 500, depth lowers 2-local test error but raises 2-global test error. T. Mori et al., 2020 ↗
Pruning changes risk beyond parameter reduction 9 studies

Pruning and sparsity sweeps can produce additional risk minima and peaks. Their locations and benefits depend on initialization, training, label noise and distillation.

  • Generative-audio masking and trimming errors reach minima after substantial parameter removal. P. Esling et al., 2020 ↗
Held-out losses can show double descent 3 studies

Model-wise second descents can appear in held-out cross-entropy or negative log-likelihood. Their visibility depends on inference and averaging methods.

  • CIFAR-100 CNN and ResNet18 width sweeps show cross-entropy test-loss double descent without stated added noise. Lorenz Kuhn et al., 2021 ↗
Limited data can favor smaller language models 2 studies

Under severe data limits, additional parameters or repeated training can worsen held-out language-model performance during pretraining or fine-tuning.

  • With 100 million tokens, one-epoch models above 2 billion parameters underperform 200 million–1 billion-parameter models. B. Barak et al., 2023 ↗
V2Test error can fall, rise, and fall again during training 48604

Suggested status Ccontested

Several independent groups reproduce this pattern under specific training conditions, but the unqualified claim is contested. Sweeps of neural networks on tabular data fail to produce it, and adjusting step sizes can remove or reduce it.

Original resultNakkiran et al., 2019 ↗

In the original study, Nakkiran et al. tracked ResNet18 test error over training epochs on CIFAR-10 using Adam.

With 15% label noise and up to 4K epochs, sufficiently large models showed error falling, rising near interpolation, then falling again. The pattern also appeared with 20% noise and augmentation; varying-noise experiments showed that final error could fall below the first minimum.

Related findings8 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Training duration changes the benefit of capacity 15 studies

Capacity and sample size affect convergence and the best stopping time. Reaching zero label error or a late second descent need not yield the lowest test risk.

  • Longer averaged-SGD training improves synthetic random-feature generalization but remains slightly worse than minimum-norm regression. Fanghui Liu et al., 2021 ↗
Late overfitting need not recover 9 studies

Some noisy-label or excess-capacity models show late degradation without recovery within the reported training horizon. Noise, data structure and regularization affect this behavior.

  • Final error rises with label corruption; minimum error stays flat before rising at higher corruption. Yu Feng et al., 2021 ↗
Unequal learning speeds can generate temporal peaks 9 studies

Features learned at different speeds can produce epoch-wise peaks. Aligning their learning rates or regularization can remove peaks and improve the best early-stopped performance.

  • Rescaling layer step sizes eliminates CNN epoch-wise double descent and improves best early-stopped performance. Reinhard Heckel et al., 2020 ↗
Delayed generalization need not reflect interpolation 9 studies

Delayed generalization and sharp learning transitions depend on data amount, model size, initialization and separability. Their appearance does not establish interpolation-driven double descent.

  • With large initialization and small weight decay, IMDB accuracy improves long after training-set fitting. Xuekai Zhu et al., 2024 ↗
Data repetition can produce risk peaks 8 studies

Repeated or near-duplicate data can produce risk peaks and degradation associated with replay. Deduplication, data order and regularization alter the effect.

  • At fixed compute and repeated-token fraction, intermediate repetition raises evaluation loss above the no-repetition baseline. Jessica Chudnovsky et al., 2026 ↗
Feature organization changes during the second descent 7 studies

Recovery under label noise involves changes in learned representations and the organization of clean and noisy features. The proposed mechanisms differ across architectures.

  • An MLP develops a large early-layer signal near second descent as clean and noisy activations separate. Tomoki Kubo et al., 2026 ↗
Training and measurement choices change observed curves 7 studies

Learning rate, optimization coordinates, stochasticity and sample weighting can change generalization trajectories. Evaluation frequency can also affect which features of a curve are visible.

  • Equal training durations restore stability scaling across MNIST MLP widths. Jonas von Berg et al., 2026 ↗
Sparse embeddings can limit useful training 4 studies

Sparse categorical embeddings can cause abrupt degradation after one epoch in click-through-rate models. Reducing feature sparsity can extend useful training.

  • Sparse-feature removal enables stable multi-epoch CTR training after validation performance reportedly peaks at epoch one. Ergun Biçici et al., 2026 ↗
V3More training samples can raise test error near the interpolation threshold 99525

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce the effect in linear regression and synthetic neural models under specific conditions. Evidence in language models remains limited, especially for locating the rise near interpolation.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Additional data can hurt away from interpolation 8 studies

Misspecification, robust objectives or contamination can make additional samples increase risk away from interpolation thresholds. The effect depends on the learner.

  • Optimally tuned ridge has higher expected risk with two samples than one under heteroscedasticity. Preetum Nakkiran et al., 2020 ↗
Distribution shift changes the value of data 7 studies

Distribution shift changes the benefits of capacity, data and regularization. Additional training samples or longer contexts can harm performance on the target distribution.

  • For in-distribution-tuned isotropic ridge, distribution shift determines whether additional samples help or hurt. Alex Nguyen et al., 2024 ↗
Task diversity and context change scaling curves 3 studies

Task diversity and context length can shift or suppress generalization peaks. Longer context does not uniformly improve performance.

  • Training on games together removes or delays validation-loss peaks at intermediate model sizes. J. Kim, 2026 ↗
Data allocation can have an intermediate optimum 2 studies

Generalization or convergence can be best with an intermediate amount of data assigned to a stage, or an intermediate dataset size. The result depends on the task and whether training time is counted in parameter updates or full passes through the data (epochs).

  • Chest-X-ray active-learning error falls then rises as the first-stage budget share grows, under reported settings. Hugo Cui et al., 2026 ↗
V4Risk can fall again beyond interpolation across model classes 20414027

Suggested status Ccontested

Several independent groups reproduce a second descent across model classes under specific conditions. Its interpretation as a general extension of the classical U-shaped curve is contested because capacity definitions and training protocols can change or remove it.

Original resultBelkin et al., 2018 ↗

The original study varied neural-network size, random-feature dimension and tree-ensemble complexity.

The study found double descent across these model classes, including random-feature experiments with 10,000 training samples. In the tree and boosting experiments, it varied both the complexity of each learner and the number of learners in each ensemble.

minimum-norm least squares, isotropic well-specified linear model · Analyze asymptotic prediction risk as the feature-to-sample ratio γ varies. · Features: isotropic; SNR: ≤ 1; Axis: γ = p/n

out-of-sample prediction risk: For γ < 1, risk is σ²γ/(1−γ); for γ > 1, risk is r²(1−1/γ) + σ²/(γ−1). The risk diverges as γ approaches 1; for γ > 1 it decreases monotonically and approaches the null risk from above as γ → ∞. (baseline: null risk r²)

Related findings6 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

When interpolation helps or harms 37 studies

Fitting training data exactly can yield vanishing excess error (benign), bounded positive excess error (tempered), or harmful generalization, depending on dimension, covariance spectrum, signal alignment and noise. The estimator’s assumptions also matter.

  • SGD’s bounded, positive excess error tends to vanish as input dimension grows relative to sample size. Guy Kornowski et al., 2023 ↗
Interpolation guarantees depend on specific assumptions 12 studies

Generalization guarantees for interpolators depend on spectral, geometric and algorithmic assumptions. Specialized bounds can describe settings that conventional capacity arguments miss.

  • An architecture-independent bound applies to explicitly constructed zero-loss ReLU minimizers under stated assumptions. Thomas Y. Chen et al., 2025 ↗
Some learning curves improve without a peak 8 studies

Some learners and data regimes show monotone or saturating gains from additional samples, training time or width. No double-descent peak is reported in those settings.

  • LC-Net JPEG-steganalysis accuracy improves with more training images, with a fitted error floor. Hugo Ruiz et al., 2020 ↗
Tree capacity has distinct intervention axes 4 studies

Tree-ensemble curves depend on the algorithm and how capacity changes. Averaging learners and increasing the number of candidate splits can have different effects.

  • Gradient-boosted trees show double descent when candidate split counts vary, with other reported capacity settings fixed. Ryuichi Kanoh, 2026 ↗
Wider Bayesian models can predict worse 2 studies

Increasing width in Bayesian hierarchical models can degrade prediction toward an infinite-width limit. The best width depends on mismatch between the prior and target.

  • Two-layer Bayesian NNs usually maximize UCI test log likelihood at 8–16 hidden units. Geoff Pleiss et al., 2021 ↗
Generative objectives can introduce capacity peaks 1 study

Supervised objectives or pseudo-supervised objectives (using generated training targets) can introduce peaks in generative models’ performance curves as capacity increases. Objective weights and optimization methods affect the pattern.

  • Objectives using generated targets produce double descent, including in a nonlinear Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty. L. Luzi et al., 2021 ↗

How it works

V5Can one effective complexity measure predict peaks across size, epochs and samples? 1292

Suggested status Ccontested

Independent studies in restricted settings support explanations based on spectra (patterns of eigenvalues or singular values), effective rank (the number of substantial directions) and model capacity, but a single predictor across model size, training duration and sample size remains contested. Counterexamples involving error over training challenge the universal explanation without directly measuring effective model complexity.

Original resultNakkiran et al., 2019 ↗

The original study varied model size, training duration and sample size in image and translation models.

With 15% label noise, sufficiently large ResNet18 models showed an error peak over training epochs near interpolation; data augmentation shifted the CNN peak across model sizes toward larger models. For Random Fourier Features, error peaked when the number of training samples equaled the feature dimension, but these observations did not establish a single predictor across model size, training duration and sample size.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Interpolation thresholds depend on loss and effective rank 42 studies

Risk peaks can follow separability, effective feature rank or local interpolation constraints. Nominal parameter and sample totals can miss these thresholds.

  • Across sample sizes, peaks track the number of independent learned-feature directions rather than nominal width. Bruno Loureiro et al., 2021 ↗
Complexity measures track some curves 21 studies

Measures derived from training can track particular double-descent curves. Their associations vary across architectures, noise levels and metrics, leaving a universal peak predictor unestablished.

  • Pruning tolerance tracks CNN and ResNet18 test loss better than the curvature-based effective parameter count. Lorenz Kuhn et al., 2021 ↗
Norm peaks do not determine risk peaks 7 studies

Minimum-norm predictor norms often peak near interpolation and decline afterward. A norm peak can also occur when test risk is monotone.

  • The estimator norm can peak even when risk remains monotone. Xinyue Li et al., 2023 ↗
Margin bounds can fail to track test error 4 studies

Overparameterization can increase sparsity or normalized margins (scale-adjusted gaps between correct and competing class scores). Yet error bounds based on those margins may still fail to track test error.

  • Margin-based test-error bounds exceed one, missing rising and falling test error in the studied settings. Vidya K. Muthukumar et al., 2020 ↗
V6Do noise and variance explain multiple peaks removed by optimally tuned overfitting controls? 192605

Suggested status Ccontested

Independent studies support noise or variance mechanisms, multiple peaks, and removal by tuned regularization in specific settings. The general claim is contested: bias can diverge without label noise, and peaks can survive optimized input-noise regularization, although optimal ridge removes them in specified linear and random-feature settings.

Test-risk deterministic equivalent; normalized second-order effective degrees of freedom ηλ: The variance term is σ²ηλ/(1 − ηλ); at p = Ntr, as λ ↓ 0, 1 − ηλ ∝ √λ and the variance contribution grows as λ^-1/2. The peak is associated with ηλ approaching 1.

Related findings6 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Variance can rise and fall around interpolation 32 studies

Prediction variance and variability across training runs can peak near interpolation and decline with width. The pattern depends on how variance is decomposed and evaluated.

  • Standard and parallel ResNet-18 loss variance rises then falls, with descent beginning at width 8. Ryumei Nakada et al., 2021 ↗
Poor conditioning can amplify interpolation risk 24 studies

Nearly singular design, kernel or covariance matrices can amplify risk near interpolation. Conditioning alone does not establish a risk peak or vanishing excess error.

  • Random Fourier feature regression’s matrix becomes noninvertible at interpolation, then better conditioned as width grows. Luis Ontaneda Mijares et al., 2026 ↗
Extra features can induce implicit regularization 16 studies

Weak or noisy features, finite feature sampling and overparameterization can induce effective shrinkage. These effects resemble ridge regularization under the models' stated assumptions.

  • Low training-shot budgets suppress the interpolation peak and act as effective ridge regularization. Gabriele Lo Monaco et al., 2026 ↗
Risk can peak as regularization changes 15 studies

Risk can be non-monotone as explicit regularization or optimizer temperature changes. The best penalty depends on noise, spectrum, class balance and the evaluation objective.

  • A spherical normalizing flow’s reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence peaks; its maximum a posteriori curve lacks second descent. Thomas Tulinski et al., 2026 ↗
Feature order can generate multiple descents 10 studies

Feature inclusion order, target alignment and spectral learning stages can generate non-monotone or staircase risk curves. These patterns need not involve a single interpolation transition.

  • With zero noise, misordered feature inclusion produces multiple descents entirely below interpolation. Xin-Ran Li et al., 2020 ↗
Optimal ridge can be zero or negative 7 studies

Beyond interpolation, covariance alignment and implicit shrinkage can make zero or negative ridge penalties optimal. Positive ridge does not always improve risk.

  • Negative ridge improves some MNIST fits but causes diverging risk peaks in others. D. Kobak et al., 2018 ↗
V7Measuring effective parameters can turn double descent into a U-shaped curve 963

Suggested status Ccontested

The claim is contested and depends on the complexity measure. Test-time effective parameters recover U-shaped curves for trees, boosting and random Fourier features on MNIST, while another measure retains second descent in random Fourier features and random forests.

Original resultNakkiran et al., 2019 ↗

No original paper is identified for this claim.

Rethinking Parameter Counting in Deep Models: Effective Dimensionality Revisited

Linear feature-count model, generalization gap plotted against Neff (text, Fig A.6)

The generalization gap lost its second descent against Neff but varied nearly linearly among interpolating models rather than forming a U-shape.

Challenges3 sources
A measure was argued to preserve double descent by changing in one direction as dimension varied. Raaz Dwivedi et al., 2020 ↗

Revisiting minimum description length complexity in overparameterized models

Replacing parameter count with MDL-COMP on the x-axis

The authors argued that double descent persists against MDL-COMP because it is monotone in d, without plotting the relationship.

Cited measurements (1)

OLS test-error curves · The authors consider replacing parameter count with MDL-COMP on double-descent test-error plots. · Complexity axis: MDL-COMP, which the authors state remains monotone with dimension; Reference axis: Parameter count

Whether the test-error curve becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve under the alternative complexity axis: The authors state that the qualitative double-descent conclusion does not change when using MDL-COMP. (baseline: Parameter-count axis)

Section 6.1, discussion of possible causes of double descent

A complexity measure preserved second descent in random Fourier features and random forests with fixed features. Oskar Allerbo et al., 2026 ↗

Constant-feature models (RFF, random forest) with complexity measured by GAC

Test MSE retained its second descent when plotted against GAC.

The $\varphi$ Curve: The Shape of Generalization through the Lens of Norm-based Capacity Control

Capacity counted as degrees of freedom df1/df2, Frobenius norm, spectral complexity, or first-layer norm

Double descent persisted against df1/df2, Frobenius norm, spectral complexity and first-layer norm, while selected norm measures incorporating bias information removed it.

Source check disagrees: it reads this result as a limit.

Related findings1 group of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Second-descent solutions can match regularized estimators 3 studies

Some solutions beyond the interpolation threshold (where training data can first be fit exactly) match transformed first-descent solutions, linear ridge regression or low-rank regularized estimators. These equivalences do not establish a full U-shaped risk curve—risk falling then rising—under a different measure of complexity.

  • The overparameterized synthetic-augmentation limit equals kernel ridge regression with a rank-k factor kernel. Andrea Carriero et al., 2026 ↗

Measuring generalization curves

Check performance on held-out data, the metric used and the limits of the diagnostic before interpreting a peak or recovery.

Sensitivity and boundary fragmentation can peak 12 studies

Input sensitivity and decision-region fragmentation can peak near interpolation and decline afterward. Regularization or changes in data geometry can separate these patterns from test risk.

  • Lower bounds on input sensitivity rise during training, whereas sensitivity peaks when model width varies. G. Khromov et al., 2023 ↗
Representation geometry changes around generalization transitions 8 studies

Representation rank, compression and alignment across networks can change around generalization transitions. Their relationship to risk depends on noise, task and training stage.

  • Some weight-decay settings yield staged MNIST accuracy gains alongside double descent in MLP feature ranks. Si-Min Fan et al., 2024 ↗
Curvature and training dynamics can track risk 8 studies

Some risk peaks and recoveries coincide with changes in curvature, parameter displacement, connectivity or dynamical stability. These associations have exceptions across settings.

  • The study’s loss-sharpness measure tracks noisy-label validation error across widths better than the effective parameter count. Devansh Bisla et al., 2022 ↗
Evaluation metrics can disagree about overfitting 7 studies

Held-out loss, accuracy, generalization gap and ranking metrics can show different curves. Evaluation-label noise, loss geometry and calibration can change the visible pattern.

  • DeepSurv log-risk norms increasingly exceed the true log-hazard norm as training loss falls. Yin Liu et al., 2025 ↗
Interpolation and evaluation design matter 7 studies

Observing a peak depends on whether the estimator actually interpolates and whether evaluation uses unseen data. Non-interpolating models or full-data evaluation can lack a peak.

  • GIN molecular-property models retain training error and show single U-shaped test-error curves across tested dimensions. Sheng-Rui Li et al., 2023 ↗
Information criteria can diverge from test risk 7 studies

Regret and information criteria sometimes track interpolation risk. Marginal likelihood and information efficiency can follow different curves depending on priors, spectra and tuning.

  • Trigonometric interpolation has larger minimum-norm solution norms and regret near interpolation. Koby Bibas et al., 2021 ↗
Training rebounds do not establish test-risk peaks 6 studies

Optimization distance, training loss and policy entropy can follow non-monotone trajectories. These observations alone do not establish double descent in held-out risk.

  • Standard LoRA on LLaMA-2-7B shows a transient training-loss rebound that sharpens at rank 128. Yu-Peng Chang et al., 2025 ↗
Generative fidelity recovery doesn’t establish interpolation with vanishing excess error 6 studies

Diffusion memorization and fidelity depend on data, capacity, training time and score-matching regularization. Recovery in distributional distance does not establish that interpolating population scores yields vanishing excess error.

  • Rectified-flow CIFAR-10 FID and sliced-Wasserstein curves fall, rise, then fall identically across splits. Pierre Marion et al., 2026 ↗
Exponents describing kernel convergence rates can oscillate 4 studies

Kernel convergence-rate exponents and plateaus in approximation error can vary non-monotonically when sample size and dimension change together. These patterns can occur even as error decreases with sample size.

  • Spherical kernels’ optimal worst-case convergence-rate exponents alternate between peaks and valleys, distinct from error peaks. Weihao Lu et al., 2023 ↗
Estimation and training losses can differ from prediction risk 4 studies

Parameter-estimation error, loss when each example is held out in turn, and training-set prediction error can differ from held-out error. They need not peak, grow without bound, or reach their minimum at the same settings.

  • Normalized excess state-action loss on training data levels off at noise variance, without diverging at interpolation. Zaehee Kim et al., 2025 ↗

Training interventions

Ensembling, replay, training constraints and privacy perturbations can change peaks and the training choices that work best.

Ensemble design changes interpolation peaks 13 studies

Averaging, subsampling and ensemble weights can suppress peaks or change risk. An optimized ensemble under a fixed budget need not outperform a single model.

  • Score averaging beats majority vote for three random-feature logistic models; infinite ensembles erase the difference. Bruno Loureiro et al., 2023 ↗
Training interventions can shift or suppress peaks 5 studies

Structural constraints, group-fairness penalties and mutual-learning losses can shift or damp risk peaks. These effects occur beyond scalar ridge tuning.

  • Mutual learning (training models together) lowers the error peak across widths and shifts where overparameterization begins. Fumika Komori et al., 2026 ↗
Capacity and replay can reduce forgetting 4 studies

Excess capacity can reduce catastrophic forgetting. Replay-buffer size can shift the location and severity of continual-learning scaling peaks.

  • Excess-capacity MLPs retain episodes and rules better after training on interfering associations. Joshua T. S. Hewson et al., 2024 ↗
Training-loss floors change overfitting trajectories 3 studies

Maintaining a training-loss floor—a lower limit on training loss—can induce a second decline in ordinary held-out loss or suppress robust overfitting (worsening robustness on held-out data during training). The outcome depends on the objective and how the floor values are distributed.

  • Flooding prevents rising robust test loss in adversarial PrLM training; a 0.2 floor works best. Bin Zhu et al., 2023 ↗
Privacy changes training and stopping requirements 2 studies

Privacy perturbations can introduce interpolation-related singularities in training error. They also change sample requirements and optimal stopping times.

  • With differentially private gradient descent, training wider random-feature models and MNIST networks is best stopped earlier. Simone Bombari et al., 2025 ↗

Deployment outcomes

Evaluate robustness, calibration, subgroup behavior and downstream objectives separately because aggregate prediction improvements need not carry over.

Clean generalization does not ensure adversarial robustness 11 studies

Interpolation and continued training can worsen adversarial risk even when excess error on clean data vanishes. Attack norm, perturbation size, activation and stopping rule affect the outcome.

  • At radius 0.1 in Case 2, additional samples worsen SI loss but improve LP risk. Jing Peng et al., 2026 ↗
Average improvements can conceal subgroup harm 5 studies

Aggregate scaling curves can conceal harms or benefits to particular groups. Group behavior depends on spurious correlations, covariance differences, noise allocation and the training objective.

  • Under reweighted training, larger CelebA models worsen worst-group error beyond interpolation while average error improves. Shiori Sagawa et al., 2020 ↗
Capacity curves depend on forecasting and portfolio objectives 5 studies

Portfolio Sharpe ratios and forecasting losses vary with capacity in ways that depend on objectives and signals. A second improvement need not beat a simple benchmark.

  • The studied portfolios’ Sharpe ratios fall then recover as dimension, composition and target vary. Mehmet Caner Agostino Capponi Maurizo Daniele Mihailo Stojnic, 2025 ↗
Source training can shape target risk 3 studies

Interpolation in the source model (fitting all training data), along with its pretraining conditions, can shape generalization after transfer to a target model. These conditions can carry generalization patterns over to the target, delay them or reverse them.

  • The source model’s interpolation error peak also appears in targets with fewer samples than the source. Yehuda Dar et al., 2021 ↗
Calibration can diverge from prediction error 3 studies

Calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy) and uncertainty in predictions given the observed data can rise and fall or plateau while prediction error improves. These calibration and uncertainty patterns can persist with regularization chosen to minimize error.

  • ScaleCNN calibration error rises then falls with width, while MobileNetV2 calibration error rises monotonically. Mohammed Alnemari et al., 2026 ↗
Unstable reconstruction can destabilize model predictions over time 3 studies

Reconstruction that is highly sensitive to small changes can destabilize models of reduced dimension or models that feed predictions back in to predict later states. Suitable reconstruction priors (assumptions about what is being reconstructed), noise or regularization can reduce this instability.

  • More trajectories destabilize magnetic-pendulum NGRC rollouts; suitable regularization suppresses instability, with interpolation proximity unestablished. Yuan-Zhao Zhang et al., 2024 ↗
Downstream metrics can favor different checkpoints 3 studies

Out-of-distribution detection (spotting inputs unlike the training data) and downstream-task metrics can have different optimal settings or scaling curves from test performance on data drawn from the training distribution.

  • Out-of-distribution detection peaks at intermediate training checkpoints while test accuracy on the training distribution keeps improving. Jia-Ning Zhu et al., 2023 ↗
Stable accuracy can conceal individual-example forgetting 2 studies

Forgetting individual held-out examples can increase with model size or reduced data even when aggregate test accuracy remains stable.

  • ResNet18 forgets a larger fraction of held-out CIFAR-100 examples with reduced training data. Uri Stern et al., 2025 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Preetum Nakkiran et al., 2019 ↗ Deep double descent: where bigger models and more data hurt

    Compares network width, training duration and sample size, including cases where optimal early stopping prevents added samples from worsening results.

  2. 2

    Mikhail Belkin et al., 2018 ↗ Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off

    Introduces the general double-descent picture through shallow networks, random Fourier features and forests.

  3. 3

    Yi-Chen Wang et al., 2025 ↗ The $\varphi$ Curve: The Shape of Generalization through the Lens of Norm-based Capacity Control

    Independently tests width-wise double descent; plotting error against norms (vector lengths) depends on parameter ranges and how capacity is measured.

Known gaps in this draft

The main gaps concern unresolved disagreements, unmeasured thresholds for fitting training data exactly, untested mechanisms involving complexity and regularization, and uncertainty about evidence reliability or whether replications are independent.

All 7 gaps
  • Some apparent disagreements still need comparisons under matched conditions. The disagreement about noiseless logistic classification remains unresolved.
  • In the pretraining comparison of models with 1.4 billion parameters, results changed direction in ways that depended on the training setup, but no peak was established near an exact fit to the training data. What this implies for the proposed explanation based on regularization, which limits overfitting, remains open.
  • Some engineering and diffusion-distillation studies report decreasing error without locating the interpolation threshold. These trends do not establish behavior near interpolation.
  • A theoretical ceiling alone does not show whether actual test error peaks or where a peak lies relative to an exact fit to the training data.
  • Effective data rank summarizes how many directions contribute substantially to variation in the data. Thresholds based on it have not established a single measure of model complexity that predicts where error peaks.
  • Some conclusions still depend on disputed source statements or incomplete readings. Their evidential support needs verification.
  • Some studies listed as separate publications may describe the same work. The extent of independent replication remains uncertain.
